en: If not dogs, what sort of men were they?
We had brought ruin upon the Kalmyks.
We wretched ones defended the cave,
Exposed to the six villains,
Who would thus bring slaughter upon us.
Telling the camel to Jedigir
With the six villains, we wretched ones
Exchanged shots for seven days without pause.
As we fought them one on one,
Manas Khan's forty companions—
Ajibai and elder Bakai were absent—
Damn those dog-swine!
They broke into my treasury;
Those swine robbed me of so much wealth.
When blessed Manas was alive,
All forty were lions side by side;
All forty were warriors who shook the age.
They broke into my treasury with axes,
Smashed it, bringing calamity.
They made me pay a terrible reckoning.
The thick flesh over my ribs
They had that dog Kirgilchal shoot.
Sobbing, taking the shortest way,
Leaning upon them, wretched as I was,
I led these forty guards.
I mourned for Khan Manas,
Deprived of the treasury's wealth.
‘Alas, Manas, do not die!’ I cried.
‘Let my wretched life suffer no humiliation!’
To die—life is sweet;
To enter the earth—the ground is hard.
Dejected and grieving,
Deprived of the treasury's wealth,
Countless gold coins, refused when asked—
You let him seize by force.
Together we had lost the sultan.
‘Leopard Manas, dear lion,
Take us with you!’ I mourned.
Driven from the ruined court in Talas,
When I crossed the ridge toward here,
I, wretched man, made my way here.
Walking in bewilderment,
To this great grave of Khan Manas,
When I came to the great grave—
In this very grave,
While I was taking shelter,
Your elder Bölökbai grieved.
Khan Manas's forty-handled brass cauldron—
Parted from that brass cauldron,
I, Bölökbai, was truly wretched.
I had no support to lean upon.
When my warrior Manas died,
My blessing, lion Bakai, was absent.
I had no cliff beyond a goose's flight,
No inaccessible dark mountain.
My strength deserted me; I grew weak.
When I reached this place,
My eyes dimmed from loss of blood.
Leopard Manas's lionhood
Was understood at that very moment,
And the loss of one of my legs.
Limping along in sorrow—
My precious orphan, listen:
Manas Khan's sacred copper cauldron,
When I came to this place,
I suffered hardship, parted from it.
The reason I carried it—
My colt, people have ordinary cauldrons,
But one that fed the whole people,
A forty-handled copper cauldron like this,
My precious lion Manas possessed.
Thinking, ‘It will be needed to live,’
Thinking, ‘A gift left by King Manas,’
‘When I see its shape, let it be Talas,
Let it be as though I saw him himself—
My dear Manas.’
That cauldron of Manas,
I bound again and folded up,
Entrusted it to my Aisooru,
And brought it out of Talas.
The reason I brought it—
When it was hung with ‘In God's name!’
Game would come and be slaughtered;
All who looked on ate their fill.
Its handles folded eight times,
Whenever he went out to battle,
Generous Manas, the dear lion,
Loaded it upon the swift camel.
It was sacred, well proven.
Such was the nature of the cauldron,
A legacy left by my Khan Manas.
In those days, for many days and nights,
When they broke into the treasury,
When my wretched self went hungry,
Suffering terrible violence,
Left in darkest night,
My colt, I passed through Kyrchinduu,
Seeking shelter by the dark cliffs,
Urging my companions with sharp commands,
Hiding my wretched self.
When I came to this place,
I hung up the copper cauldron.
I hung the cauldron at the marked place,
Turned my face and called the azan:
‘Khizir of the road, guide me!
My companion Manas, sustain me!’
Coming this way and marking the place,
When we camped at this spot,
Whirlwind-bottomed Enteri,
When he came to this place,
When I set him on watch,
I hung my belt around my neck,
Because of our hunger,
And pleaded, crying, ‘Oh God!’
When Bölökbai searched the foothills,
Skilled hunter, wretched man—
Six hinds and three stags
Bölökbai shot and took.
Leaving out not a single shank,
When he put them into the great cauldron,
The middle of the cauldron bubbled,
Bloody foam hissed around its rim.
Just as we were to fill ourselves with pale meat,
Just as hunger was to end,
The forty swine left by Manas,
Abyke, Köbösh—the six villains—
Enteri, whom I had set on watch,
Resting on his elbow,
That swine had remained there,
Taking a little sleep.
Those dogs seized the watchman;
When they killed him and cut off his head,
Digging my pit deep,
Making my misery boil like this,
When those great dogs fell upon me,
I was plunged into terrible turmoil.
My dear orphan,
Life is sweet in this world;
I abandoned the cauldron and the boiling meat.
With my wings broken,
Like a woman stricken by an evil spirit,
I went in sorrow, wretched soul,
Parted from my cauldron.
I sobbed and coughed as I wept.
With forty guards following me,
I, wretched man, fled,
Carrying this gray short gun.
Sobbing, holding myself up,
‘My fierce Manas, take me!’ I cried,
Leaning upon the gray short gun.
‘The moon is dark; the night is clouded.
So this is what night is!
When a noble one's eyes close,
So this is what day becomes!’
Dejected, grieving,
Yet I did not die—life is sweet,
My colt, though parted from my cauldron.
Had the cauldron I relied upon been beside me,
Would I not have hunted my game?
Would I not have kept myself alive?
Had I eaten my fill, would I not have raised
A great cloud of dust against those villains?
When those dogs seized my cauldron,
That was when they settled accounts with me.
‘This villain's cauldron—
They have brought it,’ they said,
Striking it with axes, pounding it,
Abyke, Köbösh—the six villains—
That was where they smashed the cauldron apart.
My guards grieved;
They saw darkest night,
Parted from their cauldron.
Taking axes, sobbing,
‘Manas, whom we leaned upon, has died now!’
So cried the forty guards,
Each striking his own head,
Wailing and crying aloud.
Thus they settled accounts with me;
Khan Manas's sacred cauldron—
There the villains smashed it apart.
I came back once,
And saw its fragments.
I have words to speak openly:
‘If my orphan, the generous one's son,
Comes back to Talas,
I shall cast it and take an omen.
If he takes after Manas himself,
The cauldron will come out like you.
I shall measure it and take an omen.
Let me cast this cauldron;
Then let me dry my tears.’”
So saying, Bölökbai
Made his bellows ready.
He prepared plenty of charcoal.
He had the charcoal scattered like sheep.
The forty guards, accustomed to the work,
Pumped the bellows hard now.
He took an omen for the orphan.
Before this or that could be said,
In the blink of an eye,
He cast the cauldron anew.
Compared with when bloodthirsty Manas lived,
It now stood greater still.
God had granted his wish.
The poor lame smith
Had regained what he once had.
The cauldron was cast anew;
The forty guards ate their fill.
Their tears ceased.
When they saw that cauldron,
All shouted with joy,
Crying the battle cry, ‘Manas!’
Their knees bent to the ground;
All hurried up in a row.
Bölökbai and old Bakai,
All of the forty guards,
Raised their hands and sobbed,
Dedicating their wether to God,
Crying out, ‘Amen!’
Hanging their belts around their necks,
‘Keep my orphan safe!’ they said,
Pleading with God alone.
They slaughtered the gray wether now.
Into the cauldron where food would not boil,
The heroes brought it,
The wether vowed to Baabedin—
They put in all of it now.
As though leopard Manas, bloodthirsty lion,
Had come alive again today,
With Bölökbai and Bakai at their head,
And the forty guards as well,
They fell into a mighty sleep.
Resting upon their elbows,
Taking a little sleep,
Lying until their hips grew numb,
Sleeping on their sides until satisfied.
At that time, Semetey,
After everyone had fallen asleep,
For many days and many nights
The orphan slave had eaten nothing.
He rose from sleep,
What my elder, leopard Khan Bakai,
Had cooked—the bull camel's meat—
Your orphan saw it.
Making a skewer from a birch,
Manas's son Semetey
Began gulping down the meat.
Leaving the bones, he ate it all,
Ate all the gray bull camel's meat.
Kaisap left it.
‘Let elder Bakai eat,’
This rascal left not a spoonful of broth for that.
Bakai awoke from sleep,
Turned onto his right side,
Hurriedly said his prayers,
Hung his belt around his neck,
